cues.text: A new game at twelve
Sam Kerr was born in 1993 near Perth, in Western Australia.
Her father and her older brother Daniel both played Australian rules football as professionals.
Sam played that game too, when she was young.
Swap the ball.
When Sam was twelve, she switched to soccer, mostly because of rules that limited girls in Australian rules football.
It meant starting again, with a new ball, a new team and new skills to learn.
When one path closes, you can find a new one. Starting again takes courage.
Starting behind
Sam began playing soccer as a junior at the Western Knights, in Mosman Park.
Moving from Australian rules football to soccer was not easy, and she faced some struggles along the way.
But she kept going, and played three years with the Knights.
Lift the flap to see who noticed.
At thirteen, Sam was spotted by Bobby Despotovski, a striker for Perth Glory.
He called her athleticism and raw talent exceptional.
At fifteen, she played for Perth Glory, the youngest player ever in her league, and for Australia too.
Feeling behind at the start is normal. Keep practising, and people will notice.
Hurt before the World Cup
In December 2014, Sam hurt her knee and needed an operation.
The World Cup in Canada was only months away.
Turn the calendar pages.
Sam worked hard with a fitness coach, Aaron Holt, to recover.
She was ready in time, and she was Australia’s starting striker in their first World Cup match.
She helped Australia beat Nigeria 2–0, and later the team beat Brazil 1–0 and reached the quarter-finals.
Getting better takes patience. A good helper and hard work can get you back.
A season lost
Back home with Perth Glory, Sam scored the winning goal in the first game of a new season.
But it was her only goal that season.
Her ankle gave way, with nobody even touching her, and the injury kept her out for the rest of the season.
Roll the sun back up.
The next season, Sam came back and scored ten goals.
She led Perth to the Grand Final, and she won the Julie Dolan Medal, one of the biggest awards in her league.
A lost season is not a lost dream. You can come back stronger.
Watching and waiting
In 2023, the World Cup came to Australia, and Sam was the team’s captain.
But a calf injury kept her out of the first match, and then out of all three group games, while her teammates played on.
Open the tunnel gate.
Sam came on as a substitute against Denmark, and scored in the penalty shootout against France.
In the semi-final against England, she scored a goal praised as one of the best of the tournament.
Australia lost 3–1, but they had reached their first World Cup semi-final.
Cheering for your team while you wait is part of being a team.
Back from the big injury
In January 2024, at a training camp in Morocco, Sam badly hurt her knee.
It was an ACL injury, and it kept her out for the rest of the season, and for a long time after that.
Twenty months passed before she played again.
Fill the comeback bar.
On 14 September 2025, Sam finally returned for Chelsea.
She came on in the seventy-fifth minute, and in the ninety-third minute she scored her hundredth goal for the club.
Big setbacks can take a long time to heal. Keep going, and your comeback can be special.
